headline: Dhaka traffic overhaul: Karwan Bazar kitchen market to be moved to Gabtoli
summary: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has ordered a series of measures to reduce congestion, including relocating the kitchen market and Fullbaria bus terminal.
details: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has issued several directives to modernize traffic management and reduce congestion in Dhaka. A key decision was made to relocate the Karwan Bazar kitchen market to Gabtoli.

During a meeting at his Tejgaon office on Saturday, the PM discussed the implementation of an Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) system at expressways and flyovers. A dedicated app for this system is to be completed within four months.

To further ease traffic, the Fullbaria bus terminal will be moved to Keraniganj. A temporary terminal will be built on 15 acres of land in the Jhilmil project area within four months, while a permanent one is planned.

The PM also ordered the expansion of the Gabtoli bus terminal's rear section to increase capacity. Additionally, the Secretariat area's parking system will be improved, with potential parking at the Osmani Memorial Auditorium.

Regarding public transport, a new policy for auto-rickshaws will be formulated. The Prime Minister also directed that necessary action be taken against unauthorized double-decker sleeper buses operating in the city.

The meeting was attended by the Home Minister, Roads and Bridges Minister, and other high-ranking officials. The PM emphasized the coherence of various agencies to complete these tasks within the stipulated time.
caption:

During a meeting at his Tejgaon office on Saturday, the PM discussed the implementation of an Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) system at expressways and flyovers. A dedicated app for this system is to be completed within four months.

To further ease traffic, the Fullbaria bus terminal will be moved to Keraniganj. A temporary terminal will be built on 15 acres of land in the Jhilmil project area within four months, while a permanent one is planned.

The PM also ordered the expansion of the Gabtoli bus terminal's rear section to increase capacity. Additionally, the Secretariat area's parking system will be improved, with potential parking at the Osmani Memorial Auditorium.

Regarding public transport, a new policy for auto-rickshaws will be formulated. The Prime Minister also directed that necessary action be taken against unauthorized double-decker sleeper buses operating in the city.

The meeting was attended by the Home Minister, Roads and Bridges Minister, and other high-ranking officials. The PM emphasized the coherence of various agencies to complete these tasks within the stipulated time.

headline: Families of the disappeared criticize new draft law on enforced disappearances
summary: Victims' families and human rights activists call for independent probes by the National Human Rights Commission instead of security forces.
details: A seminar organized by the human rights organization 'Odhikar' in Dhaka brought together families of victims of enforced disappearances and those who had returned.
Attendees expressed anger and grief, with some claiming that new disappearances are still occurring under the current government.
The 'Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Remedy Act' draft was heavily criticized, with some calling it a 'rotten law' that could facilitate more disappearances.
Critics, including MP Mir Ahmad Bin Kasem, argued that the draft allows security forces to investigate their own, which they believe is not neutral.
The draft law also includes a provision where an accuser could face up to five years of rigorous imprisonment if the court deems the allegation false.
Human rights activists demanded that the power to investigate disappearances be handed to the independent National Human Rights Commission.
They also called for the legal ability for families to manage the bank accounts and properties of the disappeared, and the withdrawal of false cases against those who returned.
The event took place on the eve of the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, observed on August 30.
caption:
Is the new law protecting victims or the perpetrators? Families of the disappeared call the draft law 'rotten'.

A seminar organized by the human rights organization 'Odhikar' in Dhaka brought together families of victims of enforced disappearances and those who had returned.

Attendees expressed anger and grief, with some claiming that new disappearances are still occurring under the current government.

The 'Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Remedy Act' draft was heavily criticized, with some calling it a 'rotten law' that could facilitate more disappearances.

Critics, including MP Mir Ahmad Bin Kasem, argued that the draft allows security forces to investigate their own, which they believe is not neutral.

The draft law also includes a provision where an accuser could face up to five years of rigorous imprisonment if the court deems the allegation false.

Human rights activists demanded that the power to investigate disappearances be handed to the independent National Human Rights Commission.

They also called for the legal ability for families to manage the bank accounts and properties of the disappeared, and the withdrawal of false cases against those who returned.

The event took place on the eve of the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, observed on August 30.
